The Baelama anchovy Thrissina baelama is a small-bodied clupeiform that reaches a maximum total length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm], a size that positions it among the smaller members of the family Engraulidae. This species is widely distributed across the tropical Indo-Pacific, where it forms large coastal schools and supports local artisanal fisheries. The larvae emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs after a brief incubation period; at a water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the time from fertilisation to eclosion is approximately three days [ab = approximately three days]. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva, measuring less than three millimetres in length, carries an extremely small wet weight at birth of about 0.00031 grams [Wwb = about 0.00031 grams], a mass that underscores the highly fecund, low-investment reproductive strategy characteristic of many small pelagic teleosts. Upon hatching, the prolarvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves, with first exogenous feeding occurring roughly two days later as the yolk becomes fully absorbed.

Sexual maturation in Thrissina baelama occurs at a total length of 11.3 cm [Lp = 11.3 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 13 grams [Wwp = approximately 13 grams]. This length threshold, observed consistently across several populations in Southeast Asian waters, marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the HPG axis. At the species' typical environmental temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a mature female can achieve a maximum reproductive output of approximately 9.2 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 9.2 offspring per day], a rate recorded in individuals measuring 12.7 cm in total length and reflecting the species' capacity for sustained, batch-style spawning across extended breeding seasons. This elevated daily fecundity, coupled with a relatively rapid maturation schedule, allows the anchovy to capitalise on ephemeral pulses of planktonic productivity characteristic of its nearshore habitat.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Baelama anchovies has been estimated at 40.7 grams [Wwi = 40.7 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions on field-collected specimens of maximal size. This asymptotic mass, reached only by the largest individuals approaching the species' maximum total length of 16 cm, reflects a life history trade-off between rapid somatic growth and the high energetic demands of continuous reproduction. The age at birth, corresponding to the hatching interval, is three days [ab = three days] when maintained at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a brief embryonic phase consistent with the small egg size of this species. The egg itself has a diameter of 0.84 mm, and the calculated birth mass of 0.00031 grams [Wwb = 0.00031 grams] is a direct consequence of this minute yolk volume.

Under the warm thermal regime typical of tropical coastal environments (28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate of Thrissina baelama reaches about 9.2 eggs per day [Ri = about 9.2 eggs per day] for a female of 12.7 cm total length. This figure, derived from laboratory spawning trials, indicates that a gravid individual can release hundreds of eggs over the course of a single month. The life span of this species is approximately four years [am = approximately four years] when reared at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a relatively short longevity that is typical of small, fast-growing clupeiform fishes with high natural mortality rates. Field mark-recapture studies in the Philippines have confirmed that few individuals survive beyond their third breeding season, with senescence and post-reproductive mortality becoming evident after the fourth year of life.

In the coastal ecosystems it inhabits, the Baelama anchovy plays a critical trophic role as a planktivorous forage fish, converting copepod and zooplankton biomass into energy readily available to larger piscivores including mackerel, tunas, and sea birds. Spawning behaviour is characterised by multiple nocturnal releases of pelagic eggs over an extended reproductive season, with individual females capable of releasing several thousand eggs across successive spawnings. Egg diameter has been measured at 0.84 mm, and the chorionate embryos undergo cleavage and gastrulation within a single day of fertilisation at the prevailing thermal conditions (28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]). The extended spawning window allows the species to exploit seasonal pulses in primary productivity, ensuring larval survival during periods of peak prey abundance in the nearshore planktonic community.
